# Human machine teaming in mobile miniaturized aviation logistics systems in safety-critical settings

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Gwendolyn Morgan a, Martha Grabowski b,\*

a Cognitive Science Department, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, New York 12180-3590, USA

b Department of Industrial & Systems Engineering, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, CII 5229 110 8th Street, Troy, New York 12180-3590, USA

## A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords: Uncrewed aerial systems Human factors System performance Human performance Situation awareness

## A B S T R A C T

Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and autonomous systems allow machines to increasingly function as teammates with their human partners, rather than as tools used by the humans. As teammates, machines share team goals, act to achieve those goals, and coordinate those actions with other teammates. Autonomous systems and AI herald new capabilities in human machine teams (HMTs) in which plans, activities, communications, and decisions are guided by intelligent technology, advanced computation and sensor systems, and a combination of human and automated decision makers. Uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) in HMTs, or mobile miniaturized aviation logistics systems (MMALs), have stretched the reach and impact of logistics systems, transporting critical supplies, equipment, parts and material, often to remote locations with minimal infrastructure. Although researchers have often considered MMALs’ impacts in safety-critical systems, there is increasing interest in understanding the role of AI and automation in HMT, and in empirical research and theoretical models that directly address the impacts of HMTs that incorporate MMALs. To address these needs, we present a framework and research project evaluating autonomous and AI-enabled UAS in human machine teams. We describe use of the framework in a case study of Arctic emergency response and logistics operations and conclude with needs for future research.

## 1. Introduction

Uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) in human machine teams (HMTs) have been deployed in various settings, such as search and rescue and Arctic oil spill response [1], healthcare deliveries [2], emergency management and humanitarian efforts [3]. UAS in HMTs, or mobile miniaturized aviation logistics systems (MMALs), have stretched the reach and impact of logistics systems, transporting critical supplies, equipment, parts and material, often to remote locations with minimal infrastructure [4], as in global vaccine transport in remote locations [5], and in the response to Hurricane Helene in the U.S. in October 2024 [6]. MMALs can play an important role in remote and infrastructure-poor settings, where they can provide timely and life-saving supply distribution, leveraging machine learning-enabled operations and communications [7], and effecting autonomous UAS mobility [8] with artificial intelligence (AI), broadening the system's temporal and geographical reach [9].

MMALs have introduced new capabilities, but also new challenges. MMALs face traditional logistics constraints, including weather, environmental, political and technological limits [9], as well as new cybersecurity vulnerabilities and privacy concerns with the integration of facial recognition software [10]. Public concerns about increased UAS surveillance, remote communication interception and listening, and the potential for hacking [10] can impede MMALs operations and acceptance. Traffic conflicts in congested disaster response areas [11] and integration challenges in the national airspace [12] suggest the need for careful consideration of human machine teaming using MMALs, especially given recent needs in remote and infrastructure-poor settings [13].

Although researchers have often considered MMALs impacts in safety-critical systems, addressing team-centered processes and metrics and workload and decision-making [14], few studies have considered the role of MMALs AI and automation on human performance [15], or have considered the impact of human or team performance on UAS technical performance [16]. Almost none of these studies have been undertaken in remote and infrastructure-poor settings.

Our research highlights needs for understanding and evaluating human machine teaming in logistics systems, with a focus on MMALs in remote, safety-critical settings. We present a framework for HMT evaluation in logistics systems incorporating autonomous and AI-enabled

The framework is grounded in the technology-to-performance chain (TPC) and human machine teaming (HMT) literature, highlighting human machine teaming challenges in MMALs with embedded intelligence. We present an illustrative case study of Arctic emergency response and logistics operations as an example of these challenges in remote settings, and conclude with needs for future research.

## 2. Background

Mobile miniaturized aviation logistics systems, comprising networks of UAS organized to transport goods, supplies, and resources, play an increasingly important role in logistics for humanitarian and disaster operations [17]. Networks of cooperating UAS can extend logistics systems’ reach and range [4], improve delivery of critical material [18], adapt to changing connectivity and infrastructure needs [19], assist with emergency response [4,17], and improve operational effectiveness and resiliency in remote and harsh environments [9].

Research in networked logistics systems such as MMALs has often focused on system performance [20], with operator performance and perceptions less studied, although some work has addressed the physical, mental, and psychosocial aspects of human factors in logistics [21,22]. Some studies have considered the impact of UAS automation and AI on operator fatigue [23], as well as on UAS operator education and training needs [24]. Significant causes of UAS accidents have been attributed to a lack of operator situational awareness, decision-making, and skill-based errors, as well as improper setup, coordination, and handover processes [25]. Human machine team performance workload increases with UAS have been shown to differ based on crew position or level of automation [26], as well as on how tasks are delegated to automation, especially with multiple UAS operations [27]. Thus, some research has addressed systems and operator performance impacts in MMALs, but little work has focused on technology performance and human performance together, or their integration, particularly in remote and safety-critical settings [28], or in systems with advanced technology [29].

MMALs increasingly incorporate autonomy and $\mathbf { A } \mathbf { I } ,$ using a wide array of technologies and capabilities, including computer vision, to identify three-dimensional structures [30], as well as to improve mobility and communication in search and rescue missions [31]. The advent of autonomous systems and AI in complex, large-scale logistics systems highlights the need for better understanding of human machine teaming models, human-autonomy teams [32], and human-AI teams [33,34] in these settings, a motivation for this research. To address this need, this research extends previous work by examining how MMALs impact human, system and team performance and perceptions together in remote, safety-critical settings and proposes a theoretical lens through which those impacts can be considered.

## 3. Research model

Our work is motivated by the lack of theoretical models and empirical studies that directly address the impacts of HMTs that incorporate MMALs. Although some research has assessed how different automation levels impact operator, system, and team performance [35,36], fewer studies have undertaken in situ empirical research [36], particularly in remote and challenging settings. To address this research gap, we propose expanding upon the TPC [37] with the HMT literature, examining the impacts of MMALs on system and operator performance and perceptions in remote, safety-critical systems.

Our research model (Fig. 1) explores how technology characteristics, including levels of autonomy and AI, impact operator, system and human-machine team performance and situation awareness in safetycritical systems. Each of these characteristics has been studied in other safety-critical systems, but seldom have all variables been considered together in a comprehensive framework, or integrated so that the impacts of the variables on each other are considered. In Fig. 1, technology characteristics, including levels of autonomy and embedded AI, are expected to positively impact UAS system performance, consistent with earlier studies [8,38,39,40], and operator performance with UAS, although previous operator performance results have been mixed [9,25, 41]. The model builds from this baseline and then explores whether technology characteristics will positively impact human-machine team performance [33,42,43,44], and human-machine situation awareness (SA), drawing on Endsley's SA model and others [15,42,45–48]. Important to a full understanding of human-machine technology impacts, the model also examines how operator characteristics and perceptions, as well as social and environmental factors, moderate the impact of technology characteristics on UAS and human performance, human-machine team performance, and operator situation awareness [9, 14,36,41,49–51]. Novel considerations are the inclusion and integration of the impacts of UAS performance on operator and team performance, as well as on operator and team situation awareness.

The TPC model [37] (Fig. 2) is foundational to our research model and to our understanding of how technologies impact users. The TPC model integrates human performance research linked to task-technology fit (TTF) with research on user attitudes as predictors of technology utilization and impact, suggesting that for a technology to have a positive impact on human performance, the technology must fit with the tasks it is to support, and it has to be used. Task-technology fit impacts have been investigated by many researchers in various settings [52], and linked positively with user self efficacy [53], and negatively with stress [54,55] and workload [56]. These studies often focused on business, office and simulated environments, utilizing variables that reflected those settings, including production timelines, training and ease of use [57]. More recent studies have concentrated on education and healthcare settings, linking TTF with social constructs, stress and workload, particularly in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic [54]. Cautions about the generalizability of TTF studies suggest that fit variables need to consider domain settings to avoid questions about validity across contexts [58]. TTF studies thus provide a baseline for the research model, but also suggest the need to explore broader avenues of investigation, particularly with UAS, automation and AI technology.

Aside from TPC studies, technology characteristics and levels of automation have long been considered in studies of system and operator performance, SA and workload in dynamic settings [49], including those utilizing UAS [59]. UAS performance studies, in contrast, have often focused on technical challenges, such as UAS lost links and hardware system failures [60] and cybersecurity attacks and hijacking [61], with some work focused on UAS-human team or operator performance [62, 63], but little research focused on the impact of AI on UAS-human team performance [64]. In this study, we are particularly interested in understanding both human and technology performance impacts and perceptions when operators are using novel technology, the central tenets of the TPC model. This is particularly apropos given the dearth of empirical research exploring autonomous and AI-enabled technology such as MMALs in remote, safety-critical settings, and the importance of technology and human performance in logistics systems, particularly those in remote locations. Our research also extends the TPC model to include the roles of stress, workload, self efficacy, situation awareness, and other human factors impacts and perceptions, in a setting that has been little explored. These gaps motivate our research in a unique, remote, and safety-critical environment using the lens of an extended TPC model, while also integrating understudied human factors considerations.

The integration of situation awareness with human factors, operator and system performance and perception metrics is a case in point, addressing the lack of attention given to the integration of human factors, particularly situation awareness, in previous studies. Although technology capabilities matched to tasks and autonomous processes have been suggested to improve both system and operator accuracy [38] and efficiency [8], few studies have integrated considerations of how operator, team and system performance impact operator situation awareness [45]. Thus, although many studies have individually considered UAS system, operator and team performance, little research has integrated considerations of these variables with human factors, situation awareness and operator perceptions, particularly in infrastructure-poor or safety-critical settings.

HMTs incorporating autonomous UAS provide a rich locus of research interest. Some studies examining the ability of HMT partnerships to leverage autonomous decision-making and self adaptation capabilities [46] have been undertaken, and studies have shown success with UAS operators off-loading tasks to automation, to AI or to a UAS, to reduce workload during missions [65], and with AI-copilots providing real-time guidance to UAS operators and teams, increasing operator situational awareness and performance [16]. Studies of the development of shared SA between human and AI teammates with UAS have addressed the nature of human machine teaming [66], leveraging earlier work examining the impact of varying AI levels of automation (LOA) on workload and human SA [47]. SA studies of operators using UAS with embodied AI have considered impacts on human-machine performance, including how adaptive autonomy could increase an operator's situational awareness [67]. Important to a full understanding of human-machine technology impacts are considerations of how operator characteristics, perceptions, and expectations, as well as social and environmental factors, moderate the impact of technology characteristics on UAS and human performance, human-machine team performance and operator situation awareness $[ 9 , 1 4 , 3 6 , 4 1 , 4 9 - 5 1 ]$ . Novel considerations are the inclusion and integration of the impacts of UAS performance on operator and team performance, as well as on operator and team situation awareness.

Despite previous research, therefore, little empirical work has integrated findings on the impact of human machine teams utilizing AI and autonomy in UAS in safety and logistics systems, leveraging TTF, TPC and human factors research, and very little research has integrated human operator, UAS and team performance impacts using autonomous and/or AI-enabled MMALs, especially in remote settings. Equally understudied are the influence of operator characteristics and perceptions, as well as external social and environmental factors, on operator, UAS system and team performance, as well as on situation awareness. The next section presents a setting where such examinations are critical, a case study of HMTs using MMALs with varying levels of autonomy and AI in the remote and infrastructure-poor setting of Arctic emergency response.

## 4. Case study – MMALs in Arctic emergency response

Increasing economic, scientific, military, transportation and tourist activity in the Arctic is occasioning the need for logistics planning, response and resource allocation [68] for both commercial and military purposes. As Arctic activity increases, so do concerns about risks to personnel, the environment, and to national security, all of which can occasion the need for Arctic emergency response (AER) [69]. Effective AER is particularly challenging due to the lack of critical infrastructure, technology and communication systems in the Arctic, all of which are necessary to provide timely response in this fragile, pristine and rapidly-changing ecosystem. In the Arctic, the harsh climate; lack of information, communications and transportation infrastructure; sparse population; and the enormous distances between villages; coupled with the unpredictability of the weather and the magnitude and power of sea states and environmental conditions complicate access to material, personnel and information, and can delay deployment and supply of critical resources. Public expectations for four-season response capability in the event of an incident in the Arctic also increase the need for timely and effective AER [70].

AER operations rely on a network of distributed organizations with limited resources, transportation options, and technology in an often unforgiving natural setting. Response operations are the primary responsibility of the U.S. Coast Guard; the Alaska Air National Guard; state and federal environmental and resource protection agencies; and are supported by a host of other organizations, including Canadian provincial and national organizations; military resources; private and non-profit response organizations; Alaskan community, borough and native organizations; as well as members of the Arctic Council [69,71]. AER activities are carried out by these cooperating groups and organizations on foot through harsh and often snow and ice-covered terrain; or using snow machines on ice roads constructed by spraying firehoses on snow-covered ground; or utilizing the limited number of tracking and location technologies, helicopters and fixed wing aircraft available in the Arctic [69]. Given the lack of Arctic population centers, runways and landing sites, and the extreme climate and difficult geography, many areas of the Arctic are treacherous to access, even if technology, personnel and material were available. Moreover, response efforts in this fragile and changing ecosystem demand the use of sustainable and low environmental impact technology and solutions [9,72]. The use of MMALs, a lightweight, relatively low cost, environmentally sustainable, resilient and mobile technology, to supplement existing AER resources offers the possibility of a force and solution multiplier for AER [9,72,73].

The setting within which MMALs for AER are deployed, however, has changed in recent years, as major oil companies, who were key partners supplying logistics resources, personnel, equipment and training, largely abandoned drilling operations in the Arctic between 2012 and 2014 [74]; this has led to restructured response networks [75], and an increasing use of autonomous, uncrewed and increasingly intelligent technology to supplement human resources [72,76]. Restructured response networks also occasioned redefinitions of tasks, responsibilities and requirements in AER, with organizations and individuals assuming multiple roles in fluid organizational structures in a setting where the physical environment and climate are also changing [77].

Lessons learned from the use of MMALs following Typhoon Merbok in western Alaska in September 2022 [72,78–81], and in Arctic village landslides and permafrost failures [82] and personnel rescues [72] suggest the importance of technology and human teams in AER. During the emergency and disaster response for Typhoon Merbok, the U.S. Coast Guard, the Alaska State Police and the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) deployed small, decentralized response teams using UAS for aerial surveillance, search and rescue, damage assessment, mitigation estimates and emergency response [79,80]. The visual capabilities provided by UAS-based imagery provided key input for the disaster response command and control organization, as well as to the distributed teams [78]. Given the lack of road infrastructure in the Arctic, the UAS extended search and surveillance capabilities and hours beyond those that could be supported with foot or all terrain vehicle-based activities [78]. UAS flight performance and deployment were impacted by wind and weather, delaying and preventing aerial flights, and response teams worked long hours in inclement and harsh weather without breaks [81], highlighting the importance of considering workload, effort and stress in studies of UAS in AER. The UAS extended operator situation awareness and improved system and operator performance by taking thousands of high-resolution photos paired with GIS to compile and identify the extent of damage to infrastructure, safety, and pollution threats to the community before action was taken [78]. These images were shared with disaster command leadership as well as with the community, providing increased opportunities for shared situation awareness and decision-making among command leadership, response teams and community stakeholders [78,80].

Extending these experiences suggests that autonomous, collaborative UAS [83] could address personnel and equipment limitations, extending the reach, range and response time of limited federal, state, local and regional emergency and disaster response resources [9,17]. Autonomous UAS for surveying and collecting baseline storm, physical and environmental data [39]; for intelligent planning, forecasting and search [84]; and to deliver response equipment, medical supplies, parts and critical housing, berthing, sanitary and protective equipment, also offer promise [9].

Technologies, however, are only one component in effective AER. As, or perhaps more, important are the cooperation and collaboration of the myriad agencies and individuals involved in AER [68,69]. As AER networks increasingly incorporate UAS with autonomy and embedded intelligence, new patterns of knowledge sharing, validation and trust building will be required among AER partners [77,85], which will expand models of human machine teaming in the coproduction of disaster management and emergency response activities [86]. Understanding the impact of human machine teaming in AER will thus require integration of human, technology and human-AI teaming performance with key social and organizational processes, such as knowledge sharing, co-production and boundary-spanning activities [87]. The evolution of AER to include autonomy, AI and human-automation teaming will thus clearly present research and operational challenges, a focus of this research.

Effective AER requires attention to social and organizational processes, incorporating traditional and indigenous knowledge, historical information, and community consultation [88] in the coproduction of disaster and logistics response processes [89]. Indigenous and traditional knowledge not only provides long-term historical perspectives and lessons learned, but also an understanding of the connections between people and the environment, all of which are critical to effective logistics operations and emergency response in this setting [90,91]. Knowledge of wildlife and seabird migration paths and patterns, along with deep knowledge of subsistence living, food preservation and consumption, could improve MMALs team sustainability and efficiency over long-duration distribution efforts, rescues and responses; location, tracking and personnel extraction activities could be improved by leveraging centuries-old community search and rescue patterns and knowledge [89,90]. Closely held information about the location of family and tribal hunting camps, which could serve as evacuation, staging, warming and replenishment points for MMALs operations in sparse wilderness, and in snowy and harsh mountainous settings, could also improve AER. Traditional knowledge of observed environmental changes, their patterns over time, and expected impacts, including permafrost melting, infrastructure vulnerabilities, and early or vulnerable ice break ups, could also inform MMALs safety and security planning, saving lives and improving both AER rescuer and rescued safety. These understandings, linked with new technology developments, have long been called $\mathbf { f o r } ,$ with little progress in implementation [91].

Effective coproduction of AER knowledge and processes requires integrating technological knowledge with scientific, social and stakeholder input, including developing communities of practice and boundary-spanning organizations [87]. MMALs can help fill human capital and capacity gaps in small Arctic villages and boroughs [72,92], but the acceptance and use of AI-enabled and autonomous MMALs will require attention to technology adoption research [93], as well as knowledge of how to honor and utilize traditional knowledge in an AER environment where natural forces and long histories play an important role. Local communities and First Nations seek the benefits in terms of employment opportunities, social mobility and technology innovation associated with MMALs introduction and use, as they bear the costs and challenges in terms of noise pollution, wildlife and subsistence economy disruptions, and the loss of traditional indigenous knowledge with the introduction of AI-enabled and autonomous UAS. Although pilot projects utilized MMALs to provide improved access to medical care, supplies and equipment for remote Arctic communities during COVID-19, few studies evaluated the impact of MMALs or AI-enabled UAS on traditional and indigenous communities, practices and knowledge, a clear research gap. Calls have long been heard for greater participation by indigenous communities in technology innovation evaluations and in Arctic emergency response networks, as well as for thoughtful and increased incorporation of local and traditional knowledge in AER [91,94,95], a long-standing research gap.

## 5. HMT evaluation in Arctic emergency response

The advent of MMALs in AER thus offers promise, as well challenges, particularly as human machine teaming with autonomous and AI systems grows. The Fig. 1 research model explores how technology characteristics, including levels of autonomy and AI, impact operator, system and human machine team performance and situation awareness in safetycritical systems; it also explores the moderating influence of operator characteristics, perceptions, expectations, and social and environmental factors on those relationships. We consider these research questions in light of Arctic emergency logistics using MMALs in remote locations in a research project utilizing UAS for logistics, humanitarian and disaster response, in partnership with the U.S. Coast Guard Sector Western Alaska and U.S. Arctic, and with the State University of New York (SUNY) Upstate Medical University's Autonomous Machines Department ‘Air Upstate’.

Effective AER using MMALs requires understanding how technology characteristics, including levels of autonomy and embedded $\mathbf { A } \mathbf { I } _ { z }$ impact UAS performance in safety-critical systems. AER teams are increasingly deploying UAS with varying levels of autonomy, including automatic return to base, homing and target tracking capabilities for transportation and deliveries, as well as for search and rescue, which can extend the hours and capabilities of UAS and AER teams [49,29,96], as shown in the use of MMALs in the Typhoon Merbok response [78,81]. MMALs utilizing different levels of automation have been shown to influence UAS performance, and MMALs activities can benefit from automated and pre-planned search routes, automatic imagery capture and processing, or package delivery, optimizing UAS battery life, logistics planning and UAS performance. Embedded intelligence in AER MMALs can provide beyond range of human audio or visual capabilities, identifying distress sounds or signals, mirroring wildlife and seabird search or location-finding patterns, or integrating information on-board, satellite and land-based sensor systems, all of which could optimize UAS performance, provide time-critical information, and increase the accuracy and success of logistics and search operations, perhaps decreasing time in the field [13].

AER using MMALs thus require understanding how technology characteristics, including levels of autonomy and embedded AI, can support different missions and operations to increase efficiency and success, impacting operator performance. Generally, using automation to highlight or integrate information has been found to improve operator performance and reduce workload, although if automated or AI systems are difficult to use, an operator's cognitive workload can be increased [97]. Adaptive automation and AI in AER could improve operator decision making by integrating multisensory information in real-time and integrating it with on-board imagery, offloading team members' tasks to automation or AI [65], perhaps reducing AER response teams' cognitive workload [38,49]. Automated and pre-planned search routing, automatic imagery capture and processing, or package delivery, and automated assessment of operational and mission activities, could optimize UAS operations and improve operator and team efficiency and effectiveness.

Technology characteristics, including levels of autonomy and embedded artificial intelligence, have been found to influence human machine team performance in safety-critical systems through thoughtful UAS interface [98] and team design [33]. Adaptable HMT automation has positively impacted team performance, responding to operator, task, or environment changes [99], which is critical in emergency and disaster management and extreme environments [100]. AER using MMALs could improve supporting mutual goal development, information sharing, pooled and optimized resource allocation, and shared task and mission execution by human and technology agents [33]. Studies in dynamic situations requiring varying levels of HMT autonomy and AI in have shown that team cognition can contribute to shared team understanding and positive performance, although frameworks and models to guide research are needed in safety-critical and other settings [15,101].

Understanding how levels of autonomy and embedded AI impact human machine SA is equally important in safety-critical systems where situation awareness is shared between human and technology partners. Novel technology, including autonomy and embedded AI, has shown improved human machine situation awareness [42,48], as well as team performance [43,102]. In AER with MMALs, human and technology agents jointly develop mission plans and tactics, share domain intelligence and information, jointly develop mission plans and tactics based on their perception, comprehension and projection of that intelligence and information, and execute shared tasks in support of AER missions. Autonomous and AI-enabled MMALs could serve as a force multipler in such settings, extending vision and sensor-based information gathering capabilities of AER teams, providing new insights by integrating information beyond lines of visual sight and human hearing, enhancing individual and team task and mission SA, and the development of requisite plans and operations. Benchmarking and understanding what human-machine performance and shared situation awareness look like in extreme settings with novel technologies such as AI are important research directions from which AER networks could benefit.

Interactive AI features that enable cooperative team task performance and confirmation of decisions, feedback, and measurement of performance have been shown to improve SA with UAS [43]; in MMALs and AER, this could include image recognition of specific people, buildings or locations [103], determining the status of emergency operations [104], search and rescue activities [13], and natural disaster response [105]. These technology factors and impacts are the focus of a growing number of studies in safety-critical settings, particularly as autonomous UAS and AI-enabled technology proliferates [106]. These results and suggestions are balanced, however, with studies in mixed initiative settings, where humans and autonomous agents collaboratively work on tasks, as results have shown increased operator error rates, difficulty in maintaining SA, and inappropriate trust in autonomous agents [43]. Understanding the impact of levels of AI support on operators' and their autonomous teammates’ SA, and how that varies in harsh environmental settings or with interrupted technology support in extreme weather, could be helpful in AER teams using MMALs as they consider tradeoffs between technology support, workload and fatigue [33].

One area receiving inadequate study is motivational for this research. In Arctic emergency response, social, cultural and organizational factors play an important role in impacting research, technology use and acceptance [88,91,107]. Historical distrust of technology introduction in Arctic communities has permeated discussions and projects introducing new technology, whether cell phones, geographic information systems or broadband networks [108], due to historically unequal power dynamics between communities, intersectional and overlapping forms of inequity, and community and colonial power and disruption [109,110]; the threat of eroding local knowledge systems [109]; as well as the lack of indigenous peoples’ inclusion in policy and decision making that introduced new technology to the Arctic [111,112]. Arctic social, traditional and community-based organizations have expressed distrust in new technology roll outs, in part because of the factors cited above.

At the same time, local, social and organizational knowledge in Arctic logistics is critical, as it provides insight and historical experience associated with procuring and effecting shipping, delivery, rescue and resource protection in a region with sparse human and transportation resources [111,112]; in the MMALs context, that information can be key to identifying UAS and payload siting, launch and recovery areas and paths that are accessible; to effectively performing reconnaissance, search and distribution tasks using local knowledge of weather and wind patterns, ice levels and types; and to seeking out and avoiding community and wildlife behavior and migration patterns that can assist or detract from logistics efforts, such as hunting periods and practices, polar bear dens and feeding patterns, as well as caribou and elk herd movements and access routes [113,114]. Incorporating diverse knowledge and broader understandings of social and cultural influences on human and team performance can not only improve knowledge of the impacts of new technology, but can also lead to innovation, expanding the evidence base and creating opportunities for increased trust in decision making [115–117], a desirable benefit in AER networks and teams.

Despite these projected benefits [117,118], however, there are few empirical studies that integrate local and indigenous knowledge considerations with traditional measures of human and team performance in AER, and especially few with MMALs, including considerations of when and how to operate, where to fly, and how to interact with local communities and elders, honoring traditions and centuries-old indigenous relationships with the physical environment. Understanding the importance of social, organizational and cultural factors, thus, is key in MMALs, including understanding the role of tribal alliances, borough relationships and community engagement and trust in influencing logistics system success and MMALs performance [107]. These gaps clearly motivate this research.

In contrast, much previous work has focused on the role of operator characteristics, perceptions and expectations in moderating and improving UAS performance, especially with increased workloads, or high levels or stress [36,50]. For instance, possessing a certain aptitude and cognitive ability to multitask when working with autonomous systems has shown to be beneficial for human machine teams [51]. Environmental factors, including noise, temperature, wind and potential icing, are considerations important in moderating human operator and UAS performance, especially in extreme conditions [9,119]. In AER, operator characteristics, perceptions and expectations, along with social, organizational, cultural and environmental factors, are important constructs in studies exploring the role and impact of technology in HMTs, and in this context, in MMALs for AER.

## 6. Research challenges, future work

Previous research suggests that much work lies ahead in understanding the roles and impacts of MMALs in HMTs in safety-critical systems. Table 1 summarizes Fig. 1 research variables, as well as the research challenges and gaps identified in this and previous research, all of which are foundational in future studies examining HMT in MMALs in remote and safety-critical settings.

Varying levels of autonomy within and among UAS [29] and degrees of UAS adaptability have been shown to have impact on system and human performance [96], particularly with respect to vigilance and automation dependence in multi-UAS scenarios [50]. AI and human transparency [120], explainability [121], and degrees of integration [28] will also be of increasing importance. AI and autonomy may improve UAS capabilities [40], and may result in new UAS protocols, requirements and regulations [122]. Explainable AI interfaces for human machine teaming [44] could improve trust in the UAS and in MMALs, if the user's trust level and their understanding of the MMALs' capabilities are aligned [123]. However, frameworks for evaluating the impact of intelligent MMALs and mature metric models for human machine teaming are still needed, along with empirical work assessing human and technology performance in extreme settings such as AER.

Interest in evaluating UAS system performance and operator performance will continue, accelerated by technology, geopolitical, and environmental concerns [9,124]. Future studies will also need to address human – machine teaming issues such as shared situational awareness [15, 46] and trust between human and technology teammates [46,125]. More importantly, future research will need to integrate findings across research studies, developing more robust understandings of the impact of system and operator performance, particularly in extreme settings.

Restructured AER networks that occasioned redefinitions of emergency response tasks, responsibilities and requirements, will also herald a reconsideration of task-technology ‘fit’ in a fluid organizational and task environment [77]. Little empirical work has explored how task-technology fit understandings evolve over time, particularly in remote or infrastructure-poor settings such as AER, where roles, responsibilities and technology are all changing, in an environment that is similarly in ecosystem and climate flux. Thus, the basic tenets of the TPC model, which are fundamental to many technology introduction studies, may bear revisitation in settings such as AER, where the technology, organizations and responsibilities are fluid.

Social, organizational and cultural factors will play an increasingly important role in technology introduction in safety-critical settings, and in AER that utilize MMALs. Increased attention to the impacts of unequal power dynamics between groups and organizations, including intersectional and overlapping forms of inequity [108,109], could lead to studies documenting the benefits and challenges of incorporating diverse knowledge in AER in MMALs, and broader understandings of the importance of cultural and social influences on human and technology performance in AER. Studies that explicitly address the impact of incorporating local, social, cultural and organizational knowledge in AER and in MMALs might consider the role of place-based research, knowledge co-production and boundary-spanning artifacts and processes [87] as research areas of interest. Acknowledging the technology and community disruption effects of MMALs and MMALs research, and providing social and technology antidotes, such as community-based programs that link traditional knowledge and new technology introduction as employment pathways, and that also honor long-standing traditions [107,110], might be topics of future research interest stemming from these understandings.

In some settings, such as those that are remote and infrastructurepoor, integrating and coproducing logistics systems, emergency response and disaster management knowledge to benefit and build trust among community members, stakeholders and regulators will require careful processes [77,90], as shared interorganizational knowledge is critical to effective operations [71]. MMALs incorporating AI, autonomous technology and smart contracts may therefore face a host of challenges, since knowledge sharing and trust in analog systems may have been developed over time in human-to-human socialization through shared decision-making, incident response activities, training, learning and debriefs [89]. New human, physical and technology infrastructure may thus be required for MMALs with autonomy and embedded AI, including reliable social and algorithmic transactions, and a new social infrastructure of human–machine training, learning and recommendation validation [126]. Important to evaluating MMALs with advanced technology in remote settings, therefore, will be consideration of sociological, cultural and organizational factors such as trustful long-term relationships and sustained funding support [87].

Operator characteristics and demographics will clearly change over time in this fluid operational and organizational setting. As a result, prior studies examining the moderating influence of operator confidence [41], satisfaction [127], workload [128], efficiency [106], trust [28] and self efficacy [129] on operator and technology performance in remote settings, will require careful study. As environmental and weather forces change over time, the influence of external factors, such as ambient wind, temperature, weather and other environmental conditions on human, technology and human machine teaming will also continue to be of research interest [9]. The impact of these operator characteristics and perceptions, and environmental forces, in the context of human-AI teaming in a remote setting, will clearly offer rich research avenues in the future.

Human machine teaming in MMALs, particularly in remote and infrastructure-poor settings, therefore, presents a number of research challenges and opportunities. Intelligent MMALs provide structures and settings within which important questions about human machine teaming can begin to be addressed. As MMALs with autonomy and embedded AI expand, myriad research questions sparked by human-technology teaming will likely also expand. Theoretically-grounded research frameworks and empirical studies can thus provide guidance for researchers and practitioners, and will be of continuing research interest.

Arctic emergency response networks are an example of systems using MMALs with manifold challenges, since the networks that girds most emergency response networks and that provides linkages that drive reliable and resilient performance in infrastructure-rich environments does not exist in the Arctic, or in similar remote and hazardous locations. The absence of critical physical and communications infrastructure, the scarcity of human infrastructure, the paucity of baseline and longitudinal scientific data, and the challenges of capturing and leveraging local and traditional knowledge in an era of rapid ecosystem change raise questions about the viability of MMALs, or any technology systems, in AER, particularly for novel and non-routine events. The operational and environmental challenges in AER, and the increasing use of autonomous, uncrewed and AI-enabled systems, suggest the need for additional research into human machine teaming questions as these novel human and technology systems and solutions evolve.
